newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Mediators, mutineers discuss Bangui peace plan.
newsitem.headline: Mediators, mutineers discuss Bangui peace plan.

text.p: African mediators met army mutineers in the Central African Republic on Sunday to discuss their role under a peace plan to end the impoverished nation's third army mutiny in under a year.
The draft, unveiled by Malian mediator General Amadou Toumani Toure on Saturday, calls for a national unity government in the former French colony and African peacekeepers.

Mutineers said before the talks they wanted to see whether the details of the draft addressed their grievances. "We cannot sign a document without knowing what it contains," their French-trained spokesman, Lieutenant Parfait Mbay told Reuters.
He said later that the proposals went "more or less" in the right direction but added that mediators and mutineers would hold further talks on Monday.

Toumani Toure himself gave no details of the mutineers' role under the peace proposals, thrashed out during a week of round-table talks bringing together all political parties and representatives of religious groups and society at large.
"We are returning to see our brother soldiers who are in revolt in the hope of accelerating dialogue so that we can find a peaceful and lasting solution," he said on Saturday.

French troops, based in the country under a defence pact, patrol the capital Bangui and form a buffer between mutineers and their foes in the presidential guard. France has welcomed the idea of using African peacekeepers.
Mutinies in April and May began over pay and conditions but turned into a campaign to oust Ange-Felix Patasse, a northern civilian politician who won presidential elections in 1993.
The latest mutiny, which began on November 15, degenerated into ethnic feuding. The overall death toll runs into hundreds.
Toumani Toure told a ceremony closing the round-table talks he would brief the presidents of Chad, Gabon, Burkina Faso and Mali and ask them to come to Bangui to sign the peace plan.
A truce between army loyalists and the mutineers, mainly minority Yakomas from the same southern tribe as former military leader Andre Kolingba, expires on January 23.
"We have weighed the vital need for a broad-based and open government of national unity in which a desire to work hard, for impartiality and sincerity are the cardinal virtues," Toumani Toure said.
"The possible and desirable presence of African forces is a mark of solidarity, of a commitment from our continent for a durable solution in the Central African Republic," he added.
The blueprint also calls for revival of a political protocol and government programme agreed after the second mutiny in May.

Presidents Omar Bongo of Gabon, Alpha Oumar Konare of Mali, Blaise Compaore of Burkina Faso and Idriss Deby of Chad visited Bangui and launched the mediation bid at the request of a Franco-African summit in Burkina Faso in December.
Toumani Toure, who toppled Mali's former dictator Moussa Traore in 1991, is widely respected for the way he ushered in democracy in Mali a year later and then stepped down.

The Central African Republic hit world headlines in the 1970s with the extravagent rule of self-proclaimed emperor Jean-Bedel Bokassa, who was toppled in a French-backed coup in 1979 and died last year.
